canonical_topic: Pacific Northwest power market and trading hubs
definition: The Pacific Northwest is a hydro-dominated region (about two-thirds of its electricity from hydroelectric production) that typically sells surplus power into California and the Southwest, with its supply heavily dependent on precipitation and snowmelt.
core_idea: The Cascade Mountains split the region into a temperate, densely populated western side (Seattle, Portland) and a cold-winter/hot-summer eastern side bordering the Northern Plains; Mid-Columbia (MIDC) is the hydroelectric delivery hub on the Columbia River, and Cal-Oregon Border (COB) is the major switching station linking the region's transmission lines near the California border.
key_points: About two-thirds of Pacific Northwest electricity comes from hydroelectric production, so surplus power availability depends heavily on precipitation
Water flow in this region directly affects California power prices
Cascade Mountain snowmelt is a major source of river water
West of the Cascades: temperate climate, major population centers (Seattle, Portland)
East of the Cascades: cold winters, hot summers, transitioning into the Northern Plains
MIDC (Mid-Columbia): delivery hub for hydroelectric plants on the Columbia River
COB (Cal-Oregon Border): major switching station in southern Oregon adjacent to California, interconnecting several major transmission lines
trading_implications: Precipitation/snowpack forecasts for the Pacific Northwest are a direct input to anticipating California power price movements via MIDC/COB flows
